# SRAM Controller Behavioral Specification

## 1. Overview

The SRAM controller provides access to a scrambling SRAM from a system bus. It exposes two bus regions:

- A memory region for read and write accesses to the SRAM.
- A control/status region for software configuration and status reporting.

The controller is responsible for:

- Keeping all SRAM contents scrambled.
- Managing scrambling key and nonce material obtained from an external key source.
- Detecting bus integrity failures and reporting fatal alerts.
- Initializing the SRAM with deterministic pseudorandom data under software control.
- Controlling whether instruction fetches from SRAM are permitted.

## 2. Memory Access Behavior

### 2.1 Normal Read and Write Accesses

The SRAM memory region must support read and write transactions from bus masters.

- Full-word writes must store the full data word along with the required integrity bits.
- Sub-word writes must preserve the bytes not selected by the write strobe and must recompute and store integrity bits for the resulting full word.
- Read data returned to the bus master must correspond to the data most recently written to that address, unless the scrambling key has been changed or a security escalation has occurred.

The memory addressing must appear linear and contiguous to bus masters, even though the controller scrambles the underlying physical address mapping.

### 2.2 Scrambling

The controller must keep scrambling enabled at all times. It must not provide a mode in which memory contents are stored unscrambled.

Scrambling must affect both stored data and address placement. This transformation must be transparent under normal operation: writes and reads to the same linear address must behave as a normal memory.

The controller must use the active key and nonce for all scrambling operations. If the active key or nonce changes, data written under the previous scrambling context is no longer recoverable and must be considered invalidated.

### 2.3 Blocking of Memory Accesses

The controller must stall memory bus accesses, rather than complete them with an error, while any of the following conditions is true:

- A key renewal request is pending.
- Memory initialization is in progress.
- A terminal security blocking state has been entered.

Once a pending key renewal or initialization completes, normal memory accesses must resume if no other blocking condition remains.

## 3. Key Management

### 3.1 Reset Key State

After reset, the controller must use a default, compile-time constant key and nonce. In this state, memory read and write accesses must be allowed.

### 3.2 Key Renewal

Software must be able to request a new key and nonce from the external key source.

When a key renewal is requested:

- The controller must request fresh key material.
- Memory accesses must be stalled until the new key material has been received.
- After the new key material is received, all subsequent scrambling operations must use the new key and nonce.
- The previous key and nonce must not be used again.

The controller must not allow software to read or directly write the active key or nonce.

### 3.3 Key Source Status

The controller must provide status indicating whether a requested key update has completed.

It must also provide status indicating whether the received key material was generated using valid, provisioned seed material. If the seed material is not valid, the key must still be accepted, but the controller must make the invalid-seed condition visible to software.

## 4. Fatal Errors and Security Blocking

### 4.1 Bus Integrity Failures

The controller must check bus integrity on both of its bus interfaces.

If a bus integrity failure is detected:

- The controller must latch the failure into status.
- The controller must assert a fatal alert.
- The controller must enter a terminal security blocking state.
- The active key and nonce must be replaced with the default reset constants.
- Memory bus accesses must be blocked.
- The terminal state must persist until reset.

### 4.2 Life-Cycle Escalation

If the life-cycle escalation input is asserted:

- The controller must latch an escalated status indication.
- The active key and nonce must be replaced with the default reset constants.
- Memory bus accesses must be blocked.
- The escalated state must persist until reset, even if the escalation input is later deasserted.

### 4.3 Initialization Consistency Failure

The initialization process must be internally protected against tampering or malfunction.

If an inconsistency is detected during initialization:

- The controller must latch an initialization error status.
- The controller must assert a fatal alert.
- The controller must enter the same terminal security blocking state used for bus integrity failures.
- The active key and nonce must be replaced with the default reset constants.
- Memory bus accesses must be blocked.
- The terminal state must persist until reset.

### 4.4 Alert Test

Software must be able to trigger a test of the fatal alert interface. A test alert must be emitted without latching any error or status flag.

## 5. Memory Initialization

### 5.1 Trigger

Software must be able to request initialization of the entire SRAM.

When initialization is triggered:

- The controller must write deterministic pseudorandom data to every memory word.
- The controller must compute and store valid integrity bits for each written word.
- The initialization data must be derived from the current nonce.
- Normal memory bus accesses must be stalled until initialization completes.

### 5.2 Interaction with Key Renewal

If initialization is requested while a key renewal is already pending, or if both are requested together, initialization must wait until the key renewal completes. In that case, initialization must use the newly received key and nonce.

### 5.3 Completion Status

When initialization completes successfully, the controller must set an initialization-done status bit.

A new initialization request must clear the done indicator until the new initialization completes.

If a terminal security blocking state is entered before initialization completes, the initialization must not be reported as successful.

## 6. Instruction Fetch Control

The controller must be able to selectively allow or disallow instruction fetches from the SRAM memory region. This control applies only to instruction fetch accesses, not to data accesses.

If the compile-time instruction-fetch capability is disabled, instruction fetches from SRAM must never be allowed, regardless of other settings.

If the instruction-fetch capability is enabled, the following behavior must apply:

- If the external OTP execution-select input is true, instruction fetches are allowed only when the software execute-enable control is true.
- If the external OTP execution-select input is false, instruction fetches are allowed only when the life-cycle hardware-debug-enable input is true.
- All multi-bit true/false inputs must be evaluated strictly: only the exact expected true encoding counts as true; any other encoding must be treated as false.

The result must be unaffected by the life-cycle escalation state for the purpose of this feature; the feature controls only the processor’s ability to execute from SRAM, while memory accesses remain subject to the blocking rules in Section 2.3 and Section 4.

## 7. Control and Status Behavior

The controller must provide software with the following control capabilities:

- Request a scrambling key renewal.
- Trigger memory initialization.
- Enable or disable software-controlled instruction fetch from SRAM, subject to the external OTP and life-cycle controls.
- Lock further writes to the key-renewal, initialization, and execute-enable controls.

The controller must provide software with the following status information:

- Data-integrity failure detected on either bus interface.
- Life-cycle escalation has occurred.
- Initialization completed successfully.
- Initialization consistency failure detected.
- Scrambling key renewal completed.
- Scrambling key seed validity as reported by the key source.

Status bits must be read-only to software and must be set or cleared only by hardware conditions or reset.

## 8. Reset State

After reset:

- Memory accesses must be allowed using the default key and nonce.
- No key renewal may be pending.
- The default key and nonce must be active.
- All status flags must be cleared.
- No initialization may be in progress.
- The memory contents are not guaranteed to have any particular value.
- Instruction fetching is governed by the reset values of the external execution controls and the software execute-enable control.
